3 duplicate ACKs: doesn't wait for RTO

A router serves many clients and sends them out to the Internet over a single link. Each user has their own access bandwidth, and the sum of all of them is much higher than the link's: the service is oversubscribed.

For example: 500 clients of 1 Mb add up to 500 Mb, versus a 100 Mb link. As long as they do not all transmit at once, it is enough. If everyone starts sending at the same time, they put a load on the link greater than its capacity.
Flow control protects the receiver. Here, what cannot keep up is a router in the middle of the path.
Full buffers, drops, and more traffic

Since it cannot carry everything it receives, the router starts filling the link's output buffers. If that intensity is sustained, the buffer overflows and the router drops packets: this is the congestion state.

To the client, a dropped segment is an acknowledgment that never arrives: it retransmits it. That retransmission adds to the traffic already there, and the load on the link grows even more.
Congestion feeds on itself: drops cause retransmissions, and retransmissions cause more drops. Everyone loses.
Each dropped segment comes back in as a retransmission, on top of the new traffic.

As traffic increases, link utilization increases. But past a certain point congestion appears and efficiency starts to fall: what users generate does not fit, gets dropped, and is retransmitted.

The ideal is to reach maximum efficiency and stay there: use the full 100 Mb all the time. The link has a cost, and it is best to always make use of it.

TCP has a congestion control mechanism to avoid reaching that point.
Beyond the link's capacity, generating more traffic does not deliver more: it delivers less.
Green: the ideal, always using the full 100 Mb
Allowed window: the smaller of two limits

The other endpoint has already given us a credit. Do we use it all up front, or little by little? That is where congestion control comes in.

TCP defines an allowed window:

allowed window = minimum(congestion window, credit)

The credit is set by the receiver (its buffer). The congestion window (cwnd) is managed by the sender itself, according to how the network responds. Even if the credit is enough for 1000 segments, only as many are sent as the allowed window says.
The credit protects the receiver; the congestion window protects the network. The smaller one always rules.
Example: the credit is enough for 16 segments, but the congestion window is 4. Of the 7 segments ready, 4 go out; the other 3 wait even though there is credit.

Slow start was the first congestion control method. When the connection starts, the congestion window is 1: even if the credit is huge, only one segment is sent.

For each acknowledgment received, the window grows by 1:

  • 1 segment → 1 ACK → cwnd = 2
  • 2 segments → 2 ACKs → cwnd = 4
  • 4 segments → 4 ACKs → cwnd = 8

The growth is exponential.
If traffic is introduced into the network gradually, it is possible to react when congestion appears.
A segment is lost: back to 1

When a segment is lost (the RTO expires without acknowledgment), the congestion window goes back to 1 and starts over.

If the host had been sending eight segments at a time and that causes congestion, the router fills its buffer and drops. The host resets the window: it goes from transmitting eight at a time to transmitting one at a time, drastically reducing its rate.

That lowers the load on the router and keeps link utilization from falling.
For slow start, every loss is a sign of congestion, and the response is to slow down almost completely.

Slow start has an unwanted effect. If all stations use it, they all grow their window at the same time until congestion occurs; when the router starts dropping, they all go back to 1 and stop transmitting together.

The cycle repeats over and over: this is global synchronization. The link goes from heavy use to little or no use.
Collapse is avoided, but at the cost of wasting the link a good part of the time.

An improvement. If the source receives a duplicate ACK (again "expecting 2"), there are two possibilities: segment 2 was delayed and will be acknowledged soon, or it was lost and must be retransmitted.

With 3 duplicate ACKs it does not wait for the RTO to expire: the lost segment is retransmitted. The fact that acknowledgments keep arriving shows the network works and packets are flowing; if none covers segment 2, it must have been lost.
Fast retransmit detects the loss earlier than the RTO.
Fast recovery: halve, don't reset to 1

Fast recovery is combined with fast retransmit and improves on slow start: it avoids going back to 1 every time a segment is lost.

On receiving the third duplicate ACK one can assume the segment was lost, but not due to congestion: the network is still delivering. Instead of resetting the congestion window to 1, it is set to half its value.

If there really is congestion, the mechanism works anyway, because the window is reduced.
The intervals in which transmission stops or the rate drops sharply disappear.

• Congestion: full buffers, drops, and retransmissions that make everything worse.
  • Allowed window = minimum(congestion window, credit).
  • Slow start: cwnd starts at 1 and adds 1 per ACK (1, 2, 4, 8…); if the RTO expires, it goes back to 1.
  • Global synchronization: everyone slows down at once.
  • Fast retransmit: 3 duplicate ACKs → retransmit right away.
  • Fast recovery: cwnd halved instead of reset to 1.

Connection, acknowledgments, credits, windows: it is the price of reliability. In the next lesson, the other transport protocol: UDP, which does none of this.
The receiver granted credit for 16 segments and the congestion window is 4. How many segments can be sent?
The allowed window is the minimum of the congestion window and the credit: minimum(4, 16) = 4.
In slow start, with a congestion window of 4, 4 segments are sent and their 4 acknowledgments arrive. What is the window now?
1 is added for each ACK received: 4 + 4 = 8. That is why growth is exponential (1, 2, 4, 8…).
What does fast retransmit do on receiving 3 duplicate ACKs?
Waits for the RTO to expire
Retransmits the lost segment without waiting for the RTO
Three duplicates indicate that the network is still delivering packets and that segment was lost: it is retransmitted before the RTO expires.
With fast recovery, the congestion window is 8 and the third duplicate ACK arrives. What does it become?
Instead of resetting it to 1 as slow start does, fast recovery sets it to half its value: 4.
The load exceeds the link's capacity: the router's buffers fill, there are drops, and retransmissions add more traffic.
